{
    "id": "08-multimodal/audio-diarization",
    "title": "Audio Diarization",
    "category": "08-multimodal",
    "level": "advanced",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Segment an audio stream into who-spoke-when turns from frame-level acoustic evidence with deterministic boundary rules so speaker attribution yields explicit, testable segments.",
    "body": "Audio Diarization Category: Multimodal | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Speaker attribution is only as trustworthy as its segment boundaries. This skill builds diarization as a rule-bound pipeline: acoustic frames carry a speaker label, consecutive same-label frames merge into turns, and every turn records its speaker, start, and end. The merge rules are deterministic so the same frame sequence always produces the same turn list. Acoustic labeling itself is delegated to a classifier; this skill governs the segmentation contract. When to Use Use when a transcript or analysis needs per-speaker attribution — meeting minutes, call analytics, or speaker-indexed search — and the output must be a reviewable turn list rather than a black-box label. Do not use for raw transcription without speakers; apply the audio transcription skill instead, and diarize its alignment if per-speaker turns are needed. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Acoustic frames with inferred speaker labels, time-ordered | | | | No | Shortest turn duration kept; shorter turns are dropped | | | | No | Label treated as no-speaker; frames with it are not merged | Procedure 1. Require frames to be sorted by start time before merging; unsorted input is rejected. 2. Merge a frame into the previous turn only when speaker labels match and boundaries are contiguous. 3. Start a new turn on any label change, gap, or boundary discontinuity; never merge acro ss gaps. 4. Apply the minimum-turn rule after merging, dropping turns shorter than the declared floor. 5. Record each turn as (speaker, start, end) with an identifier stable across runs. 6. Expose a coverage metric: total speech time minus turn gaps, so silent regions are visible. 7. Treat classifier labels as evidence, not truth: keep the label confidence alongside each turn when available. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Ordered, non-overlapping speaker turns | | | | Fraction of the stream covered by turns | | | | Turns removed by the minimum-turn rule | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Over-merge | Gap ignored between same-speaker frames | Merge only on contiguous boundaries | | Under-merge | Rounding splits contiguous frames | Compare with tolerance and normalize timestamps first | | Unstable labels | Classifier flickers between speakers | Smooth labels before merging and record confidence | | Unsorted input | Frames arrive out of order | Validate sort order up front and reject violations | | Silent regions hidden | Gaps never reported | Compute and expose coverage alongside turns | Security and Authority Boundary Diarization output identifies who spoke when; treat it as personal data. It grants no authority to act on speakers and must respect the retention and consent rules of the so urce audio in every downstream store. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s survey of speaker diarisation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_diarisation). 2. Python’s wave module documentation for reading PCM audio fragments (https://docs.python.org/3/library/wave.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Related Skills - Audio Transcription — produces the word-level content this skill assigns to speakers. - Audio Classification — supplies the frame labels the merge rules operate on. Changelog | Date | Version | Change | |---|---|---| | | v1 | Initial entry added under the owner-directed corpus expansion |"

{
    "id": "08-multimodal/audio-mixing",
    "title": "Audio Mixing",
    "category": "08-multimodal",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Blend multiple PCM audio tracks under explicit gain envelopes with sample-accurate summation, hard clipping bounds, and a measured output peak so a mix is reproducible and cannot silently exceed the output range.",
    "body": "Audio Mixing Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Mixing becomes destructive the moment gain is improvised: summed samples clip, quiet tracks get buried, and the result varies run to run. This skill treats a mix as an explicit contract — per-track gains, optional timed envelopes, a declared clip limit, and a measured peak — so the output is byte-reproducible from its inputs. It operates on in-memory PCM sample lists; codec-level or streaming mixdowns are out of scope. When to Use Use when combining two or more recorded or synthesized mono PCM tracks into one output track where loudness behavior and clipping must be decided by policy rather than by accident. Do not use for real-time streaming mixdowns or codec-domain processing; apply this contract after decoding, on sample data. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Two or more mono sample lists at identical length basis | | | | Yes | One fixed gain multiplier per track, declared before summation | | | | Yes | Hard output bound, e.g. 32767 for 16-bit audio | | | | No | Timed gain points applied per track before summation | Procedure 1. Declare every track gain and the clip limit before the first sample is summed; mixing with undeclared gains is rejected. 2. Verify all tracks share a sample rate and channel layout; resample or reject before mixing, never inside it. 3. Apply each track’s gain (and optional timed envelope) sample by sample, in a fixed track order. 4. Sum tracks sample-accurately in integer domain so the result is identical across runs and platforms. 5. Clip each summed sample to the declared limit and count clipped samples as a quality signal. 6. Measure the output peak after mixing; an unmeasured mix cannot be compared or improved. 7. Record the gain set, envelope, clip count, and peak alongside the output so the mix is reproducible. 8. Re-mix rather than normalize after the fact when the clip count is nonzero; clipping already destroyed information. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The clipped, summed output track | | | | Largest absolute sample value in the output | | | | Number of samples bounded by the clip limit | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Clipping distortion | Summed samples exceed the output range | Declare a clip limit up front and count clipped samples | | Buried quiet tracks | Gains improvised per mix | Fix the gain set before summation and record it with the output | | Rate mismatch | Tracks mixed at different sample rates | Verify a shared rate before mixing; resample or reject | | Non-reproducible mix | Float ordering and undeclared gains vary | Sum in a fixed track order with declared gains | | Unmeasured output | Peak level never computed | Measure and record peak and clip count with every mix | Security and Authority Boundary Mixing grants no authority over source recordings. Source material keeps its license and consent state; a mix does not launder restricted audio into usable output. Output loudness is a technical measurement, not a safety claim. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s overview of audio mixing practice (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audiomixing(recorded_music)). 2. Python’s wave module documentation for reading and writing PCM files (https://docs.python.org/3/library/wave.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Related Skills - Audio Classification — labels tracks before mixing so per-track policy can be applied. - Text to Speech — a common synthesized source track that follows this mixing contract downstream.     "body": "Image Super-Resolution Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Super-resolution uses a learned model to upscale an image beyond its pixel count. The model invents plausible high-frequency detail; it does not recover what was truly there. This skill covers applying SR appropriately, inspecting the output for hallucinated structure, and keeping the output labeled as a reconstruction — never as recovered evidence. When to Use Use for restoring legacy assets, enlarging crops for human viewing, and cleaning up downscaled media where plausibility is the goal. Do not use SR output for identification, forensics, medical reading, or any decision where invented detail could be mistaken for captured fact. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Low-resolution source image | | | | No | Target upscale (x2 default; x4 for very low sources) | | | | No | , , or to select the model variant | Procedure 1. Confirm the use case permits synthesized detail; refuse evidentiary use up front. 2. Select the model variant matching the content type; text and faces need the strictest handling. 3. Run SR at a power-of-two scale; larger factors by chained passes, not one extreme pass. 4. Inspect the output for hallucination signatures: invented text glyphs, warped faces, repeated window or brick patterns. 5. Keep the original untouched alongside the output; never overwrite the source. 6. Record in metadata that the image is mo del-upscaled, with model and scale named. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The synthesized high-resolution reconstruction | | | | Sharpness gain, artifact inspection summary | | | | Regions where invented structure is suspected | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Invented text or faces | Model fills in what it expects to see | Flag text/face tiles as high risk; human review | | Identity drift | Upscaled face is a different, plausible person | Refuse identification use; compare against original | | Over-sharpening artifacts | Halos at strong edges | Use conservative scale; inspect edges | | Output treated as evidence | Reconstruction believed to be capture | Label outputs and keep the original | | Noise upscaling | Sensor noise enlarged into texture | Denoise before SR, not after | Security and Authority Boundary Super-resolution output is synthesized imagery. {
    "id": "08-multimodal/perceptual-image-hashing",
    "title": "Perceptual Image Hashing",
    "category": "08-multimodal",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Compute average-hash fingerprints from downsampled grayscale data and compare them by Hamming distance so near-duplicate images are detected without byte equality.",
    "body": "Perceptual Image Hashing Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Byte hashes cannot recognize the same picture after a resize or re-encode. A perceptual hash captures visual structure: downsample to a fixed grid, threshold each cell against the grid mean, and pack the bits into a fixed-width fingerprint. Two images then compare by Hamming distance, and a declared threshold turns that distance into a duplicate decision. Face or semantic similarity is out of scope; this is structural near-duplicate detection. When to Use Use when a corpus must be deduplicated against resizes, crops, and re-encodes, and the decision must be explainable as a measured distance against a declared threshold. Do not use for semantic matching — different scenes with similar histograms compare equal; use classification or embedding retrieval for meaning-level search. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Downsampled grayscale values in row-major order | | | | Yes | Hamming distance at which two hashes count as duplicates | | | | No | Bits per hash; derived from grid length when omitted | Procedure 1. Downsample every image to the same fixed grayscale grid before hashing; grid mismatch makes hashes incomparable. 2. Compute the grid mean and threshold every cell to one bit, using a strict greater-than comparison. 3. Pack the bits in row-major order into a fixed-width integer fingerprint. 4. Compare fingerprints by Hamming distance — popcount o f the XOR — never by string similarity. 5. Apply the declared duplicate threshold and record the distance, not just the verdict. 6. Treat dark, flat, or synthetic grids as unhashable noise: their bits carry no structure and produce false matches. 7. Never edit images to force a match; if distances sit at the threshold, collect more evidence instead. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The perceptual fingerprint of the grid | | | | Hamming distance between two hashes | | | | Threshold-applied verdict, recorded with its distance | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False positives | Flat or low-contrast images hash to noise | Flag degenerate grids and exclude them from matching | | Grid mismatch | Images hashed at different resolutions | Downsample everything to one fixed grid first | | Threshold guessing | Cutoff tuned on unlabeled data | Calibrate the threshold on labeled pairs and record it | | Bit-order drift | Cells packed in inconsistent order | Pack row-major in one documented order everywhere | | Semantic overreach | Different scenes counted as duplicates | Keep the decision structural and confirm borderline pairs | Security and Authority Boundary Perceptual hashes are derived features of their source images; they inherit every access restriction of the source . A hash that survives deletion of the original can still identify it, so retention policy must cover hashes too. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s overview of perceptual hashing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceptual_hashing). 2. Python’s statistics module documentation for mean computation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Related Skills - Image Classification — answers what an image shows; this skill answers whether two images are structurally the same. - Object Detection — localizes content whose regions can be hashed for targeted deduplication.
